tldr: A system that automatically builds highly accurate, physically stable, simulation-ready 3D environments directly from a single photo via an interactive loop between a VLM agent and a physics simulator.
hero_caption: Overview of SceneRig and its robotics applications. From a single input image, an agent collaborates with a physics simulator to construct an editable, physically stable 3D scene (top). It achieves far higher reproducibility than the existing SimFoundry baseline in simulated evaluation of real-robot policies and open-loop trajectory replay of recorded manipulations (bottom).
overview:
Evaluating robot action policies (control models) on real hardware requires enormous equipment costs, human labor, and trial time. Large-scale evaluation in simulation is widely anticipated as a solution, but manually recreating diverse real-world task environments inside a simulator is extremely challenging. While recent approaches reconstructing 3D spaces from a single photo have attracted attention, merely looking visually similar is not enough to run a robot. If objects penetrate each other or hover in the air, running physics calculations in the simulator causes objects to instantly fly away or slide off, destroying the original layout.

To address this, the authors propose "SceneRig," a new system that directly couples a VLM (vision-language model) agent with a physics engine. The core insight here is that instead of having the agent guess and tweak raw coordinate numbers, it runs an "edit-and-validate loop" using vision tools, bounding box search tools, and feedback directly from the physics simulator itself.

Tested across 80 diverse tabletop scenes—including real-robot environments, simulator images, and smartphone photos—scenes built by SceneRig passed physics tests 100% of the time, overwhelmingly outperforming existing methods in both visual appearance and 3D placement accuracy. Furthermore, placing and running robot models in the reconstructed environments accurately predicted real-robot successes and failures, dramatically boosting the success rate of open-loop replays of recorded manipulation trajectories from 36% to 80%.
contributions: Proposed "SceneRig," an agentic system that reconstructs 3D scenes from a single image with a focus not only on visual similarity, but also on physical stability and simulation readiness for robot actions.
Constructed a modular "edit-and-validate loop" framework that directly links the VLM agent's visual reasoning with geometric search and a physics simulator (PhysX).
Significantly improved single-image Real-to-Sim performance, raising open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode outcome agreement with real-robot policies from 54% to 69%.

sections.heading: Can we build robot-ready environments from a single photo? Tackling the gap between appearance and physics
sections.summary: Because evaluating real-robot policies is expensive, simulation-based evaluation is highly desirable, yet manual environment building does not scale. Existing single-image 3D reconstruction methods suffer from objects shifting and workspace collapse under physics simulation; this work solves the issue via an integrated loop of agent reasoning and physical validation.
sections.details:
In robotics research, evaluating the robustness of learned action policies is one of the biggest bottlenecks. Real-robot evaluation remains the trusted gold standard, but it demands expensive hardware, constant human supervision, and numerous trials, making it extremely difficult to scale. While evaluation in simulation has attracted attention, the labor required to build realistic environments inside a simulator stands in the way.

Recently, "Real-to-Sim" research—automatically generating simulation spaces (digital twins) from real-world images—has made great strides. However, simply creating visually pleasing 3D scenes is insufficient for robotics. If an object slightly penetrates a table or hovers above it, turning on gravity in a physics simulator instantly causes it to slide, roll, or topple, shifting away from the robot's intended initial setup.

Even with powerful models like the latest GPT-6 Astra, merely applying post-hoc physics settling cannot recover a stable arrangement. SceneRig therefore establishes a harness that tightly couples the agent's visual reasoning with geometric and physical tools, iteratively refining placement discrepancies while executing a physics simulator. This successfully achieves both visual fidelity and physical consistency.

sections.heading: At the intersection of single-image reconstruction, VLM agents, and Real-to-Sim
sections.summary: 3D object and scene reconstruction from single images, as well as VLM-driven 3D generation, have progressed rapidly. However, methods that account for physical grounding—ensuring scenes function properly in a physics simulator for robot motion evaluation—remain extremely limited, and SceneRig fills this exact gap.
sections.details:
Related research can be broadly divided into three streams:

- Single-image 3D scene reconstruction:
Traditional supervised learning methods, CAD model retrieval (such as ROCA), and generative approaches (such as SAM3D) predict individual object meshes and layouts from single images. However, they prioritize visual fidelity and do not guarantee the physical stability required for robot interaction.

- Agent-based 3D scene generation:
Techniques employing large vision-language models (VLMs) to generate Blender code through critique-and-refine loops (such as VIGA and SEIG) have emerged. Yet, these largely restrict verification to rendered image aesthetics and coarse geometry, stopping short of precise pose correction coupled with a physics engine.

- Physically grounded Real-to-Sim:
Approaches creating interactive environments from video or LiDAR scans exist (such as RialTo and SimFoundry), but most rely on video input or multi-view captures. Even recent single-image methods (such as REST3D and TableVerse) perform contact-surface optimization or post-hoc simulation settling; none feature an agent actively diagnosing placement errors and invoking tools while monitoring the physics simulator's behavior like SceneRig.

sections.heading: A four-stage pipeline: from relation extraction to physics-grounded pose refinement
sections.summary: SceneRig adopts a staged approach: relational grounding and initial placement, background/material/lighting construction, and physics-grounded object pose refinement. Rather than relying on the agent guessing raw coordinates, it iterates between search tools and physics simulator checks to achieve millimeter-accurate, stable placement.
sections.details:
SceneRig's pipeline proceeds systematically through the following stages:

### 3.1 Relational Grounding and Metric Initial Placement
First, a VLM inspects the image to propose movable objects ($\mathcal{O}$), supporting surfaces (tables, floors, walls, denoted as $\mathcal{R}$), and a support relation hierarchy (scene graph) defining what rests on what. Next, MolmoPoint identifies keypoints for each object, and SAM3 extracts high-precision segmentation masks. The monocular depth estimation model MoGe-2 predicts camera-frame 3D point clouds, defining an absolute metric coordinate frame aligned with gravity. Object meshes are generated by SAM3D and initially aligned to the point cloud. A key insight here is "parent-to-child sequential physics settling." Dropping all objects at once causes explosive collision-driven scatter; instead, objects are grounded in Isaac Sim (PhysX) sequentially starting from those closest to the table, with drift corrected via ICP (point cloud registration).

### 3.2 Agent-Driven Background, Material, and Lighting Setup
Once objects are settled, background walls, table geometry, surface materials, and lighting are configured within a shared Blender environment. Here, a geometry agent, a material agent, and a lighting agent operate in sequence. Crucially, geometry creation incorporates a rule-based deterministic gate (check_rules). Programmatic checks strictly verify that tables do not penetrate walls and objects do not hover; only scenes passing these checks proceed to the Verifier agent, preventing failures caused by hallucinations.

### 3.3 Physics-Grounded Object Pose Refinement
Initial placement still leaves subtle visual discrepancies from the camera viewpoint. The system therefore launches an agent-led "investigate-and-edit loop." The agent uses an Investigate tool to compare rendered views of specific objects against crops of the real image, diagnosing whether the size is off or the position has shifted. However, having the agent directly write code such as "move x by 5 cm" leads to failure, so it invokes a dedicated Move tool. The Move tool performs global-to-local search using silhouette matching and DINOv2 features to find optimal translation, scale, and yaw candidates. It then tests these candidates in the physics simulator to verify they do not topple or drift excessively. A proposal is adopted only if it passes the physics test and improves the alignment score.

From a single image, it constructs a scene graph and performs parent-to-child physics grounding, builds the background using geometry, material, and lighting agents, and then iteratively refines object poses using a refinement agent equipped with a physics-verified Move tool.

The geometry stage specifically requires passing a strict rule check (Rules Gate) to prevent physical interpenetrations.

sections.heading: Benchmark evaluation: demonstrating 100% physical stability and superior 3D placement accuracy
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across 80 scenes ranging from synthetic data to real-robot environments. SceneRig passed a 5-second physics simulation across all scenes without collapse (100% stabilization success rate), significantly outperforming competing baselines in both visual fidelity (PSNR, LPIPS) and 3D object location error (OSPA).
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation utilized 80 scenes: 44 simulator images from RoboDojo and RoboLab (with ground-truth 3D positions and object meshes) and 36 images from real environments, web sources, and smartphone captures. Baselines included VIGA (a leading VLM-based 3D generation method), SceneConductor (point-cloud-based), REST3D (optimization-based), and SimFoundry (a prominent video Real-to-Sim method). Claude Opus 5 was adopted as the default VLM. Evaluation metrics included full-image fidelity (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, nCLIP), masked object-region metrics (indicated with an asterisk), 3D layout error measured by OSPA (5 cm and 10 cm thresholds), and "physical stability," evaluated by whether objects moved less than 50 mm and remained at rest after 5 seconds of PhysX simulation.

### 4.2 Reconstruction Quality and Stability
SceneRig earned the top ratings across source-view and novel-view appearance metrics, as well as VLM pairwise head-to-head judgments (Bradley-Terry scores). Most notably, regarding physical stability, while VIGA and SceneConductor failed across many scenes due to objects sliding off or blowing up upon collision, SceneRig passed the test in all 80 scenes (100%). It also dominated other methods in object-region appearance (LPIPS* 0.170) and 3D positional alignment (OSPA@10 of 1.50 cm, F1@10 of 0.865).

### 4.3 Ablation Study Insights
Using raw poses predicted by SAM3D resulted in 69% of objects penetrating supporting surfaces and 15% floating. While settling these poses afterwards with a 5-second simulation achieved stability, objects shifted noticeably, sharply degrading 3D accuracy. Furthermore, allowing the agent to edit coordinates directly through code without the Move tool (Code edits only) noticeably degraded placement precision, cutting the subsequent robot trajectory replay success rate in half from 80% to 44%. When swapping the backbone to GPT-6 Astra, SceneRig's harness significantly outperformed both VIGA and a general coding agent (Codex) running on the exact same model, proving that the design of the physical tools—not raw model capability alone—is the decisive factor.

sections.heading: Robotics applications: 69% agreement on real-robot policy evaluation and an 80% leap in open-loop trajectory replay
sections.summary: To determine whether the reconstructed digital twins are useful for practical robotics research, tests were run on two tasks: real-robot policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay. Compared to the strongest baseline, SimFoundry, SceneRig accurately reproduced real-world outcomes.
sections.details:
To confirm whether the simulation environments are truly usable for robotics, two experiments were conducted using a bimanual robot.

### 5.1 Real-to-Sim Policy Evaluation
Trained policies $\pi_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA 2.0 were evaluated across 5 tabletop tasks. Scenes were reconstructed from head-camera images across 100 total real-robot episodes (50 trials per policy), and the exact same policies were executed in simulation to test outcome agreement. The episode outcome agreement between real execution and simulation improved substantially from SimFoundry's 54% to SceneRig's 69% (statistically significant at $p=0.017$). Furthermore, the task-level correlation of success rates (Pearson's $r$) rose from 0.84 to 0.92, showing that policy capability can be accurately gauged in simulation without requiring real-robot runs.

### 5.2 Open-Loop Trajectory Replay
This experiment replays 25 successful human-teleoperated trajectories (joint angles and gripper commands) directly in the reconstructed environments without closed-loop feedback. Because trajectories are not adapted, even millimeter-to-centimeter errors in object placement or size lead to failed grasps or placements. SimFoundry successfully replayed only 9/25 trajectories (36% success rate), whereas SceneRig achieved 20/25 (80% success rate). SimFoundry frequently suffered from issues like fusing a plate and an apple into a single combined mesh—making lifting impossible—while SceneRig accurately segmented and placed individual objects, faithfully reproducing the recorded manipulations.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: bringing the entire physical world into simulation
sections.summary: SceneRig is a breakthrough system capable of constructing robot-ready 3D spaces from a single image. At the same time, challenges remain for the future, including severe occlusions in whole-room scenes, PBR texture fidelity, and handling articulated or deformable objects.
sections.details:
This work paves the way toward reconstructing physics-ready digital twins from a single photograph. By harmonizing visual realism and physical consistency, it establishes a foundation for low-cost, large-scale robot policy evaluation without physical hardware.

However, several clear limitations and avenues for future work remain:

- Scaling from tabletops to complex room environments: The current system primarily targets tabletop setups; reconstructing whole rooms dramatically increases difficulty due to viewpoint occlusions, depth ambiguities, and complex contact relations.
- Lack of physically based rendering (PBR) textures: Relying on SAM3D for mesh generation limits the fidelity of physically realistic PBR materials, leaving room for improvement in photorealism.
- Non-rigid object representations: The current system models all dynamic objects as single rigid bodies and cannot reproduce articulated links like drawers and doors, nor deformable objects such as cloth and ropes.

Future developments will benefit from integrating stronger monocular depth estimators, image-to-3D generative models, and articulation estimation.

sections.heading: Appendix: implementation details and efficiency via prompt caching
sections.summary: The appendix details multi-stage fallback mechanisms for robust object detection, Blender-to-Isaac Sim (USD) export pipelines, and context management techniques that dramatically reduce token consumption during inference.
sections.details:
Several engineering designs underpin SceneRig's robust operation:

- Hierarchical Recovery of Object Masks:
To handle missed detections or merged segmentation masks, a fallback pipeline tries full-image prompts, local crops, and point prompts in sequence. If candidate masks differ in area by more than a factor of two, the VLM resolves the ambiguity, thoroughly preventing catastrophic parsing errors.

- Long-Context Optimization via Prompt Caching:
Repeated agent edit loops risk exploding context lengths, causing severe API costs and latency. SceneRig summarizes past action histories into single sentences, discards older images, and anchors static system prompts and source images before the cache boundary. Consequently, 84.1% of input tokens during pose refinement are served directly from the prompt cache, achieving practical speeds and costs.

- USD Export Pipeline:
Scenes finalized in Blender are exported to Universal Scene Description (USD) format with baked materials and intact physical properties, including collision meshes and masses. This enables immediate PhysX simulation inside Isaac Sim without any manual adjustments.

takeaways: "Visually similar 3D" and "simulation-ready 3D" are entirely different; a validation loop involving a physics simulator is essential to prevent scenes from exploding under gravity.

Having a VLM agent directly edit millimeter-level 3D coordinates in code is ineffective; an architecture optimizing visual and geometric features through a specialized search tool (Move) is far more capable.
High-fidelity Real-to-Sim from single images makes hardware-free policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay practical with high reliability (80% success rate).
limitations: All dynamic objects are currently modeled strictly as single rigid bodies; articulated furniture (e.g., drawers) and deformable objects (e.g., cloth, ropes) cannot be reproduced.
Because mesh generation relies on SAM3D, photorealistic physical textures via PBR materials remain limited.
While highly accurate on tabletop scenes, reconstructing entire large rooms with severe occlusions and blind spots remains challenging.
